lead: A process control loop holds one physical variable — oven temperature, tank level, line pressure — at a set point the operator chooses. The loop measures the variable, compares it with the set point, and uses a power converter as the muscle that pushes the process back. Such loops run heat-treatment furnaces, boiler drums, water tanks and chemical reactors. A plating bath held at 60 °C all shift is one example.
prereq: You need: phase-angle and integral-cycle AC voltage controllers (AC-AC converters), and controlled rectifiers for DC drives.

sections.h3: The loop: sensor, transmitter, controller, actuator

blocks.text: Only a few universities teach process control inside a power electronics course. Four parts form the loop, joined one way and closed by feedback.

items: Sensor: PT100 resistance thermometer, thermocouple, float switch or pressure transducer.
Transmitter: converts the reading to 4–20 mA. Current survives long cables, and 4 mA is a live zero, so 0 mA means a broken wire, not a cold oven.
Controller: compares the measurement with the set point and outputs 0–100 %.
Actuator: the power stage — thyristor power controller, solid-state relay, contactor, variable-frequency drive or valve.

blocks.text: On-off control switches fully inside a band and lets the temperature cycle. Proportional control makes the output proportional to the error; the proportional band is the error span that sweeps the output from 0 to 100 %. Integral action removes the steady error. Derivative action damps overshoot.
A heater is the simplest load. P = V<sub>rms</sub>²/R, so the controller only sets the RMS voltage across R.
On-off control uses a contactor: cheap, but cycles last minutes, temperature swings widely and contacts wear.

Phase-angle control fires the thyristor at angle α after each zero crossing. Output moves smoothly every half cycle, suiting fast loads such as infrared lamps, at the cost of harmonics and radio interference.

Integral-cycle (burst) control gates whole mains cycles at zero crossings over a fixed period, often 0.4 s, which is 20 cycles at 50 Hz. Each burst is whole sine cycles, so there are no switching harmonics, but the on-off pattern draws current in bursts, which can flicker lights on a weak supply and makes the heater see bursts of full power.
V<sub>rms</sub> is the RMS output voltage, Vs is the RMS supply voltage, α is the firing angle in radians with 0 ≤ α ≤ π, and the load is resistive.

sections.h3: Liquid level control and pump drives

blocks.text: A tank level loop keeps water between two marks or at a set level. The simplest form is on-off: two probes or a float switch start the pump at the low mark and stop it at the high mark. The gap between the marks is the hysteresis band; it stops the pump from starting many times a minute. The pump is switched by a contactor or a solid-state relay, with a dry-run cut-out that stops it if the sump is empty.

For a steady level, a level transmitter (pressure or ultrasonic) sends 4–20 mA to a PID controller, and the controller sets the speed of the pump through a variable-frequency drive. A transmitter that spans 0 to 2 m and reads 12 mA shows (12 − 4) / 16 = 50 %, a level of 1.0 m.
Q is pump flow, H is the head, P is the shaft power and N is the pump speed (the affinity laws of a centrifugal pump).

Speed control saves energy because power falls as the cube of speed: at 80 % speed the pump gives 80 % of the flow for 0.8³ = 51 % of the power. A throttling valve gives the same flow cut but leaves the motor running near full power.

sections.h3: Sizing the heater control and the rest of the plant

items: From the rating, R = V²/P: 2 kW at 230 V gives R = 26.45 Ω and full-load current P/V = 8.70 A.

Each thyristor of the pair carries one half-cycle: its RMS current is 8.70 / √2 = 6.15 A and its average current √2 × 8.70 / π = 3.92 A. Rate the voltage at 2 to 2.5 times the peak √2 × 230 = 325 V, so 800 V devices are a common choice.
Add a fast fuse and a heatsink. Each thyristor drops about 1 V, so it dissipates about 1 V × 3.92 A ≈ 4 W, and the pair about 8 W.
Take the 4–20 mA measurement into the controller and use its 0–100 % output as the firing angle or duty cycle.

blocks.text: A PLC scans inputs, runs ladder logic and drives outputs; SCADA shows the same data to the operator as trends and alarms. Optocouplers or relays isolate the sensor circuit and the 4–20 mA loop from the power circuit, so a shorted heater cannot destroy the controller.

A variable-frequency drive holds V/f constant so motor flux stays fixed as speed changes, using a three-phase inverter; a DC drive takes its armature voltage from a controlled rectifier. Four-quadrant operation lets a drive run as a motor or as a brake in either direction of rotation, so a crane can lower a load under control. Fans, pumps, conveyors and extruders are the usual plant loads.

spec.aria: Set point and measured temperature meet at a summing point; the PID controller sets the firing angle of a thyristor pair feeding a 26.45 ohm heater; a PT100 and transmitter feed back 4 to 20 milliamperes.

examples.question: A 2 kW, 230 V heater is fed from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply through a thyristor AC controller. The load is resistive. Find R, and the firing angle and RMS current at 50 % and at 25 % power.
steps: Power fraction: p = P / P<sub>full</sub> = V<sub>rms</sub>² / V<sub>s</sub>², so V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>s</sub> √p, and the bracket in the V<sub>rms</sub> formula must equal p: 1 − α/π + sin 2α / (2π) = p.
50 %: the bracket must be 0.5. At α = π/2 = 90°, 1 − 0.5 + sin 180° / (2π) = 0.5, so α = 90° and V<sub>rms</sub> = 230 × √0.5 = 162.63 V.
examples.answer: R = 26.45 Ω; at 50 % power α = 90° and I<sub>rms</sub> = 6.15 A; at 25 % power α = 113.8° and I<sub>rms</sub> = 4.35 A.

traps: Controller output is not the firing angle: 50 % output is α = 90° on a phase-angle controller but a 50 % duty cycle on an integral-cycle one.
Heater power follows RMS current, P = I<sub>rms</sub>²R, not average current.
On a 4–20 mA loop, 4 mA is the 0 % reading of the scale; a 0 mA reading means a broken loop.
Integral-cycle control avoids switching harmonics, but its bursts still thermal-cycle the element if the period is long and can flicker lamps on the same supply.

quiz.q: Name the four parts of a process control loop.
Why is 4–20 mA used instead of 0–20 mA?
quiz.a: 4 mA is a live zero, so a 0 mA reading means a broken wire and cannot be confused with a true zero.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of integral-cycle control over phase-angle control.
quiz.a: Switching whole cycles at zero crossings gives no switching harmonics and little radio noise; the heater receives bursts of full power and the element still cycles thermally.

quiz.q: A 1 kW, 230 V heater runs at 50 % power through a phase-angle controller. Find R and I<sub>rms</sub>.
An oven overshoots each time the set point steps up. Which controller action damps this, and what does it act on?
quiz.a: Derivative action; it responds to the rate of change of the error, not to its size.

quiz.q: A crane lowers a load steadily. Which drive quadrants are in use, and why?
quiz.a: Take hoisting as positive speed and positive torque. While lowering, the motor turns in the lowering (negative) direction but must still hold the load, so its torque is in the hoisting (positive) direction: torque and speed have opposite signs, quadrant IV, braking. The load's energy flows back into the drive and is returned to the supply through a regenerative converter or burned in a braking resistor.

quiz.q: A level transmitter spans 0 to 2.5 m on a 4–20 mA loop and reads 14 mA. Find the level, and the pump power at 70 % speed if it takes 5 kW at full speed.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern plants the loop often moves into the drive: a pump's variable-frequency drive closes the pressure loop internally and the PLC sends only a set point over a fieldbus. Self-tuning PID and model predictive control sit above this layer. Search 'burst firing thyristor controller', '4–20 mA current loop' and 'four-quadrant drive'.
